paper: Bechky 2020 (Administrative Science Quarterly 65(3): 606-643; copyright The Author(s) 2019)

cards.trigger: The paper's construct of a 'comparison with DNA profiling' that all three units are said to have met (claim on pp. 606, 633, 634); the passages beneath it on pp. 617-632 differ in whether any speaker names DNA as the standard.
cards.claim: [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 606] techniques and [8 words of Bechky (2020), p. 606] alike (p. 606, restated p. 633).
cards.incumbent_reading: One comparison to DNA profiling, open to interpretation, reached each unit by a different pathway and bore on a different aspect of its work.

wager.statement: The construct does two jobs. In X passages the speaker or the quoted text itself holds other work up against DNA: the NAS excerpt sets toolmark-type tests beside [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 620] (p. 620b); an examiner at the statewide meeting says they cannot be like DNA (p. 624b); a narcotics analyst voices the demand as one made of firearms (p. 624c); Tom and Pete talk about statistics and numbers when the author asks what being like DNA means (p. 624e). In Y passages a demand is reported and the speaker names another source for it: Jason names ISO and NIST documents and scientific fields in general and denies that NAS spurred it (p. 627d); Jodi names NAS 'and other attacks', East Coast practice and the lack of an output others can review (p. 631c); Robin names a Daubert hearing on crystal testing (p. 632a); Taylor and Billie name East Coast instrument routine (p. 632d, p. 632e). In the Y passages the tie to DNA is supplied by the author's characterisation (p. 627b, p. 628c, p. 632f). Read this way, the firearms unit met a comparison with DNA, while toxicology and narcotics met demands for a stated measurement uncertainty or a reviewable output that no printed toxicologist or narcotics analyst attributes to DNA in respect of their own work. The three-way difference in response would then be partly a difference in what was asked and by whom, not three answers to one question.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: A passage in which a toxicologist, a narcotics analyst, or the defense attorney in the DUI case names DNA profiling as the standard for toxicology or narcotics work; its absence from the record behind the paper would cohere the reading, its presence would dissolve it.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Looked through the toxicology section (pp. 625-628), the narcotics section (pp. 628-632) and the methods (p. 615, where the author says interviews probed [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 615] DNA). The attorney's parallel to DNA is given in the author's voice as something he would do (p. 627b); no words of his and no testimony are printed. The phrase on p. 617 comes from a narcotics analyst but is printed without its target.

strains_against: p. 617 -- a narcotics analyst is the speaker of 'be more like DNA', and the author places it as pressure on the other subfields generally; if it was said of narcotics work, X reaches into narcotics.
p. 627b -- the author reports that the attorney's challenge would draw a parallel to DNA error measurement; if that reports what the attorney said, toxicology belongs on the X side.
p. 628c -- GC/MS logs and graphs are reported as seen as compatible with DNA standards, with no speaker given; if narcotics analysts were the ones seeing it so, DNA stands behind the Y passages.
p. 621a, p. 623c, p. 624a -- three firearms passages report pressure without naming DNA, so the Y side is not confined to toxicology and narcotics.
p. 619c -- members of other units did measure themselves against the DNA unit, though on resources and not on method.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Someone with the fieldnotes and interview transcripts from the toxicology and narcotics units, or a record of the DUI hearing.

grounded_in.bears_on: The claim that comparison with DNA profiling challenged narcotics analysts (p. 606, p. 633).
grounded_in.if_one_way: If it was said of narcotics work, the claim would read as carried by a narcotics analyst's own words and the split would weaken.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If it is the firearms remark, no narcotics analyst is printed naming DNA for their own work and the claim for narcotics would read as resting on the author's characterisation.

cards.rival: The paper's own account: DNA profiling is an informal standard with many dimensions (pp. 616-617), so error measurement and instrument output are aspects of the DNA comparison whether or not a speaker says the word, and no split is needed.

side_x.label: X: passages where the speaker or quoted text itself holds work up against DNA

side_y.label: Y: passages where a demand is reported and the speaker names a source other than DNA (accreditation and measurement documents, East Coast practice, a hearing, the NAS report without DNA)

split.separating_feature: Whether the speaker, or the document quoted, names DNA profiling as what the work is being measured against.
split.independent_of_outcome: Yes for coding: it needs only the wording of the passage, not whether the unit changed. Partly in effect, since the feature nearly coincides with the speaker's unit and unit coincides with outcome.
split.sorts_correctly: 10 of 14: the feature codes all 14 passages, and the coding lines up with the unit division (X in firearms, Y in toxicology and narcotics) in 10; the exceptions are p. 617 (X, narcotics speaker, target unknown) and p. 621a, p. 623c, p. 624a (Y inside firearms).
confounds: Unit: X passages are almost all about firearms, so the feature may only be re-describing which unit is speaking.
Elicitation: p. 624e follows the author's own question, and p. 615 says interviews probed the rise of DNA.

cards.trigger: The paper's construct of 'changing work practices', which each unit is said to have embraced or resisted (p. 606; Table 2, p. 633); the passages beneath it on pp. 621-632 concern changes of two different kinds.
cards.claim: [10 words of Bechky (2020), p. 606] its work practices (p. 606; response row of Table 2, p. 633).
cards.incumbent_reading: Toxicologists adapted their practices while firearms examiners and narcotics analysts resisted changing theirs.

wager.statement: 'Change to practice' covers two things. X is a change that leaves in place the way the result is reached and adds to what is recorded, shown or reported with it. Y is a change that replaces the person's own looking and judging as the way the identification is reached. On the X side: firearms examiners say knowing a mark on sight is no longer acceptable and images must back the call (p. 622a); they keep note packets with images of each set of striae to support judgment on the stand (p. 621b); a second examiner signs each page (p. 622b); toxicology adds an uncertainty range with the same instrument and method (p. 627a, p. 628a); narcotics analysts talk over buying microscope cameras (p. 632c). On the Y side: counting striae is not regularly used (p. 623a), numbers are declined (p. 624e), and a move to GC/MS is feared or refused (p. 631c, p. 632a, p. 632d, p. 632e). Read this way the three units look alike: each has taken on or entertained an X change, none is printed taking on a Y change, and toxicology is not printed as being asked for one. The contrast between embracing and resisting would then lie partly in which kind of change each unit was presented with. This sits close to the paper's values account for the Y passages; it departs from the paper on firearms, where an X change is printed as already made.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: The date and occasion of the firearms unit's move to image-backed documentation, and any instance of a unit accepting a Y-type change or of toxicology being asked for one.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: pp. 621-622 say firearms practices changed over time and give no date or prompt. The toxicology section (pp. 625-628) prints no request to alter the method, and Jason says it has not changed (p. 628a). The narcotics section (pp. 628-632) prints no adoption of GC/MS beyond its existing use for unknowns (p. 629).

strains_against: p. 632b -- a second analyst's visual check is an X-type change, and MCCL analysts met it with the objection that it would double the time, so X is not always welcomed.
p. 623a -- Tom does turn to counting striae when on the fence, so a Y-type tool is in partial use.
p. 624a -- the outside examiner's call to guard against bias cannot be placed on either side from the passage.
p. 624d -- the author reports that the MCCL examiners did not modify how they worked; the documentation change on p. 622a is undated and may precede the pressure.

p. 624e -- Pete's objection is to reporting a percentage, which is about how a result is stated; toxicology's change (p. 628b) also alters how a result is stated, so the feature holds only if it is drawn at how the result is reached.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Someone with the firearms unit's protocol history, or fieldnotes dating the documentation requirement.

cards.rival: The paper's values account: units accept what fits their values and refuse what does not, so X and Y only re-describe compatibility with values; and the firearms documentation change may simply predate the episode.

side_x.label: X: changes that leave the way the result is reached in place and add to what is recorded, shown or reported with it

side_y.label: Y: changes that replace the person's own looking and judging as the way the identification is reached (counting or numbers for holistic judgment, an instrument run for the crystal test)

split.separating_feature: Whether the change at issue in the passage alters how the identification or result is reached, or only what accompanies it in the record and report.
split.independent_of_outcome: Yes: the kind of change can be coded from the passage's description of the change without knowing whether the unit accepted it. One passage (Pete on p. 624e) shows the line between stating and reaching a result is not always sharp.

Cost and time: in narcotics the Y change is also the slower, instrument-limited option (p. 631c, p. 632a), and the one X change objected to is the one that costs time (p. 632b).

Elicitation: the firearms Y passage on p. 624e answers the author's question.

cards.trigger: from_pair: the court challenge facing toxicology (p. 625a, p. 627a) and the court challenges facing firearms (p. 621a, p. 624d), which the paper sets side by side on p. 635c. Several things varied: how local the challenge was (credited by the paper), fit with values (credited), a dated accreditation plan already in hand (credited only as making change easier), what the challenge was aimed at (a figure missing from a report versus the admissibility of a discipline), and an existing state-law confidence requirement (p. 627c).
cards.claim: Toxicologists were moved to change by anticipating attack on the stand, an immediate local challenge that [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 635] face (p. 625a; p. 635a; p. 635c).
cards.incumbent_reading: The local, immediate court challenge propelled toxicology's change, with the accreditation work making it easier, while distant challenges left firearms unmoved.

wager.statement: Attribute the difference to what the paper treats as a facilitator. Before the NAS report the lab was already conforming to ISO 17025, and toxicology had a three-year plan to estimate uncertainty of measurement (p. 627a). Its protocol already required a log tracing instruments, reagents and standards, and state law already required a confidence interval (p. 627c). It had quality-control data from more than five years on an unchanged method (p. 628a). On hearing of the challenge the unit brought the plan forward (p. 627a). Jason tells a criminal-justice audience that labs were not scrambling on account of NAS and that the work was already being done (p. 627d). On this reading the two units differ in whether the answer to the challenge was already scheduled by the accreditor; the nearness of the court case accounts for the date, not for the change. No comparable scheduled item is printed for the firearms unit. The reading agrees with the paper that ASCLD's requirements mattered (p. 633, p. 635a) and departs from it only in putting them first.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: What conforming to ISO 17025 required of the firearms unit and whether that unit had any dated plan of its own; and whether the DUI challenge took place.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: The firearms section (pp. 620-625) does not mention ISO or any accreditation requirement on the unit. p. 616 gives ASCLD's field-level response only. p. 627a says the lab as a whole was conforming but details only toxicology. The DUI case is described as upcoming (p. 625a) and its result is not printed anywhere in pp. 625-628 or the discussion.

strains_against: p. 627a -- the plan ran over three years and the unit chose to act at once on hearing of the challenge; if timing is the outcome to be explained, the challenge explains it.
p. 627c -- the reports in use did not yet carry the uncertainty figure, so 'already doing it' overstates what was in place.
p. 627d -- Jason's denial is made in an outreach session to the criminal-justice community, the audience from which the challenge came, so the occasion of the statement is the pressure it denies.
p. 625a -- a named local case and an attorney's campaign succeeding in other states are printed; a local threat was real.
p. 628b -- the unit's pride in the new figure fits the paper's values account as well as this one.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Someone with the lab's accreditation plan across units, or the court record of the DUI case.

passage_jobs.p. 621a: A working-group board member reports growing attempts to bar firearms evidence in pretrial hearings, the firearms half of the pair.
passage_jobs.p. 624d: The author reports that MCCL firearms testimony had not been challenged locally and that practice did not change, the firearms outcome.
passage_jobs.p. 625a: An attorney's campaign on uncertainty of measurement reaches a specific case in the lab's jurisdiction, the toxicology half of the pair.
passage_jobs.p. 627a: The ISO work and the three-year plan are dated before the NAS report and the plan is brought forward, which is the variable the reading credits.
passage_jobs.p. 627c: A tracing log, a state-law confidence requirement and existing reporting at a set confidence level show how much was already in place.
passage_jobs.p. 627d: Jason tells outsiders the unit was already doing this and was not spurred by NAS, a participant's own attribution.
passage_jobs.p. 628a: Jason describes five years of data on an unchanged instrument and method, the material the new figure was computed from.
passage_jobs.p. 628b: The unit shows pride in the new range and confidence level, which both accounts can absorb.
passage_jobs.p. 635a: The author says the unit was motivated by anticipating attack and that accreditation changes made responding easier, the ordering the reading reverses.
passage_jobs.p. 635c: The author sets the toxicology and firearms court challenges side by side, which is what makes them a pair.

grounded_in.question: Did conforming to ISO 17025 place a comparable dated requirement on the firearms unit?
grounded_in.bears_on: The claim that the immediacy of the court challenge is what separates toxicology from firearms (p. 635c).
grounded_in.if_one_way: If firearms had such a requirement and still made no change, the claim would read as strengthened: a plan in hand does not move a unit, and pathway and values do.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If only toxicology had one, the claim would read as unable to tell immediacy apart from having the change already scheduled.

grounded_in.how: Jason says the unit was already doing uncertainty measurement and that NAS did not spur it; the author says the unit was motivated to change by anticipating an attack on the stand.

same_construct: p. 635c (pathways as occasions for meaning making)

cards.rival: The paper's own ordering: the plan had a three-year horizon and the figure was not yet in reports, so without the local case it would have stayed scheduled; the challenge did the work and the plan only eased it.

cards.trigger: from_seam: the claim that each unit's technique forms its members' values (p. 626a; p. 637). The pipette passage (p. 626b) points one way; the passages on analysts leaving toxicology (p. 630b), on newcomers who do not fit (p. 626a) and on personal preference (p. 632e) point the other.
cards.claim: Toxicologists' technique instilled their values, and occupational values [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 637] (p. 626a; p. 637).
cards.incumbent_reading: Doing a unit's work produces that unit's values, which then shape how its members receive the comparison with DNA.

wager.statement: Read the direction the other way: what the paper calls a unit's values is partly a record of who came, who stayed and who left. Taylor took the toxicology job as the one that was open, did that work, wanted out, and persuaded management to train her elsewhere (p. 630b); several narcotics analysts had worked in toxicology and been eager to move (p. 630b). Neha says a 'normal person' sometimes arrives in toxicology and irritates the rest (p. 626a). Billie ties her liking for crystal tests to being a chemist and to not wanting to repeat one task, and says other people would prefer the instrument (p. 632e). Analysts are hired into a specific unit (p. 613). On this reading the same technique did not produce the same values in everyone who performed it, and the narcotics unit's dislike of standardised work would be something its members brought with them out of toxicology. The units' different responses would then track who is in them.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: Work histories for each unit showing who moved, in which direction and at whose request, and whether those who stayed in toxicology arrived with the compulsive habits they describe.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: The author says interviews covered career histories (p. 614), but only Taylor's move and the unnamed 'several' are printed (p. 630b). No toxicologist's history appears in pp. 625-628, and the firearms section (pp. 620-625) gives training length but no movement in or out.

strains_against: p. 626b -- a ruined sample brings a long report and weeks of teasing, which shows the unit teaching care on the job.
p. 623b -- Tom says his internal criteria were built through training and repeated looking, a participant crediting the work with forming his standards.
p. 630b -- Taylor says getting out took a long time, so movement between units is slow and sorting would be weak.
p. 620a -- the director treats analysts as [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 620] and plans a swap, which fits neither self-selection nor formation by technique.
p. 613 -- placement follows tests and a panel interview, and Taylor took what was open (p. 630b), so entry is not shown to follow preference.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Someone with personnel or career-history records for the lab's units, or the interview material on career histories.

passage_jobs.p. 613: Analysts are hired into a named unit after tests and an interview, which is the entry point any sorting would work through.
passage_jobs.p. 614: The author reports asking about career histories, which shows the deciding material was collected but is not printed.
passage_jobs.p. 620a: The director says every criminalist [8 words of Bechky (2020), p. 620] and plans a swap between two units, showing movement is administratively possible.
passage_jobs.p. 623b: Tom attributes his criteria to training and experience, which supports formation by the work.
passage_jobs.p. 626a: Neha describes newcomers without the compulsive habits as an irritant, which shows the trait is not universal among those who do the work.
passage_jobs.p. 626b: Jason describes the report and the teasing that follow a pipetting error, the passage that best supports the paper's direction.
passage_jobs.p. 630b: Taylor and several others did toxicology work, disliked it and left for narcotics, which shows the technique failing to instil its values in them.
passage_jobs.p. 632e: Billie grounds her preference in herself as a chemist and contrasts it with other people's, which presents the value as personal.
passage_jobs.p. 637: The author states that values follow from seeing the consequences of the technique, the claim being inverted.

grounded_in.how: Analysts who performed toxicology's technique report finding it mind-numbing and leaving; the author says the technique instils its values in those who perform it.

cards.rival: The paper's position [8 words of Bechky (2020), p. 637] (p. 620c, p. 637): whether people are formed by a unit or sort into it, the values present in the unit are what meet the comparison, so the direction makes no difference to the response.

cards.trigger: The paper leaves the narcotics working-group debate unresolved and reports the analysts' own forecast of change (p. 628c, p. 631c, p. 632b), yet closes the episode with the unit holding on to its practices (p. 632f; Table 2, p. 633).
cards.claim: Narcotics analysts met the spillover through an internal professional debate, had no immediate need to change, and so kept the practices they valued (p. 632f; p. 633).
cards.incumbent_reading: Narcotics analysts resisted changing local practices on account of their values and the absence of any direct pressure.

wager.statement: Read the narcotics outcome as where things stood when fieldwork ended in August 2010 (p. 612), not as an ending. Jodi expects the crystal test to be phased out and GC/MS to take its place (p. 631c). The working group is still debating a second analyst's check (p. 632b). The unit is weighing cameras against instruments on cost (p. 632c). Robin has attended a workshop on a recent Daubert hearing against crystal testing (p. 632a). What is printed as resistance is talk at benches and in meetings (p. 615) about preferences, time and cost; no instruction to change is printed, and no refusal of one. The objections that carry quantities are about capacity: two instruments and long runs (p. 632a), and a legal requirement of short turnaround (p. 629). If the working group ruled against the crystal test, the printed material would support reading the unit's holding on as a matter of nothing yet being required and of capacity, with values shaping how the prospect was talked about. Robin's hearing also gives narcotics a court challenge heard about at a professional event, the same shape as the one firearms examiners heard about at theirs (p. 621a), where the author records none for narcotics (p. 635b; p. 633).

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: How the working-group debate came out and what the MCCL narcotics unit did afterwards about cameras, second review or GC/MS; and where the Daubert hearing on crystal testing was held and how it was decided.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: The narcotics section (pp. 628-632) leaves the debate open, and the discussion (pp. 632-638) reports no later development. Fieldwork ends in August 2010 (p. 612). The hearing is mentioned once, through Robin, with no place or result (p. 632a).

strains_against: p. 632d and p. 632e -- Taylor and Billie object on grounds of skill and boredom, not caseload, so objections from what they value are printed.

grounded_in.how: Robin reports attending a workshop [7 words of Bechky (2020), p. 632] crystal testing; the author records that narcotics analysts met no court challenges of any kind and enters 'no' for courts.

grounded_in.question: How did the working-group debate on crystal tests end, and did the MCCL unit then change its practice?
grounded_in.bears_on: The claim that narcotics analysts' values led them to resist changing their practices (p. 632f; p. 637).
grounded_in.if_one_way: If a reviewable output was required and the unit complied, the claim would read as values colouring how a change was received, not whether it happened.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If crystal tests stayed permitted and the unit kept them unchanged, the claim would read as printed.

cards.rival: The paper's own bounded claim: during the period observed nothing required a change and the unit kept its practice, which is all 'resisted' asserts; a later forced change would not undo the finding that values shaped how the prospect was received.
